culture.title: Saying hello and goodbye
culture.note: In Germany, Austria and Switzerland, people greet each other in different ways. "Hallo" is common with friends and in relaxed situations. "Guten Tag" is a polite greeting for the daytime, for example in a shop or an office. In the evening, people say "Guten Abend". When you leave, "Tschüs" is informal and "Auf Wiedersehen" is more polite. Many regions also have their own greetings. In Switzerland you often hear "Grüezi", and in southern Germany and Austria you may hear "Servus". In polite situations, people often shake hands. Spelling a name aloud is very normal, for example on the phone or at a desk.
culture.reflection_question: How do you greet people in your language, and when do you use a polite greeting instead of a relaxed one?

mission.title: Spell your name like a pro
mission.task: Practise greeting and spelling your name aloud in German, in front of a mirror or with a friend.
steps: Say a greeting for the time of day: Guten Morgen, Guten Tag or Guten Abend.
Say: "Ich heiße ..." with your first name.
Spell your first name letter by letter in German, then spell your last name.
Say "Auf Wiedersehen!" or "Tschüs!" at the end.
mission.report_prompt: Write down the greeting you used, your name as you spelled it in German letters, and one letter that was difficult to say.
success_check: I said a greeting and my name in German.
I spelled my first name and my last name with German letter names.
mission.safety_note: Only share your name if you feel comfortable. Do not share private details such as your address or phone number.

culture.title: Saying hello and your name
culture.note: In Germany, Austria and Switzerland, people often say hello and their name when they meet. In shops, people often say "Hallo" or "Guten Tag". With friends and young people, "Hallo" is very common. Adults who do not know each other often use "Sie", but in this lesson you learn "du". People often shake hands when they meet for the first time, and they look at the other person. It is normal to say your first name first: "Ich heiße Anna." Many people also say where they are from, because it is an easy way to start a conversation.
culture.reflection_question: How do people say hello and their name in your country? Is it the same or different?

mission.title: Introduce yourself out loud
mission.task: Say three short sentences about yourself in German: your name, your country and how you are. Say them out loud to a mirror, your phone or a friend.
steps: Say: "Hallo! Ich heiße ..." with your own name.
Say: "Ich komme aus ..." with your country (for example Deutschland).
Say: "Ich bin ..." with one word, for example gut, müde or super.
Say all three sentences again without looking at your notes.
mission.report_prompt: Write your three German sentences and tell me which sound was hardest (ich, ei or ß).
success_check: I can say my name in German.
I can say where I come from.
I can say how I am.
mission.safety_note: Only share your first name and your country. Do not share your address, phone number or other private data.

grammar_vocab.prompt: Choose the correct sentence: "I come from Germany."
grammar_vocab.explanation: With "ich" the verb is "komme", and "aus" comes before the country.

grammar_vocab.explanation: The sentence starts with "Ich" and the verb is second.

grammar_vocab.explanation: "Wie heißt du?" asks for a name.

covered: You can now say your name with "Ich heiße ...".

closing.review_tomorrow: Review the forms of sein (ich bin, du bist, er/sie ist, wir sind) and practise the ich-sound.

culture.title: Phone numbers and numbers in everyday life
culture.note: In Germany, Austria and Switzerland people often say phone numbers in pairs of digits, for example 'dreiundzwanzig, vierzig, fünfzehn'. Some people say each digit one by one instead. Both ways are normal. Germans usually write the day before the month in dates, for example 3.5. means the third of May. Addresses are written with the street name first and then the house number: Lindenstraße 12. The postcode (die Postleitzahl) has five digits in Germany and comes before the city name. If you do not understand a number, you can always say: 'Noch einmal, bitte.'
culture.reflection_question: How do you say your phone number in your own language: in single digits or in pairs? Which way is easier for you in German?

mission.title: My number card
mission.task: Make a small card with your German contact details and say the numbers aloud.
steps: Write on a piece of paper: Ich bin ... Jahre alt. Meine Nummer ist ... Write the numbers as words, for example einundzwanzig.
Say your age and your phone number aloud three times. Say the phone number in pairs of digits.
Look around your home and find five numbers, for example on a clock, a package or a house number. Say each number in German.
Record yourself on your phone saying 'Wie alt bist du? Ich bin ... Jahre alt.' and listen to it once.
mission.report_prompt: Report back: Which five numbers did you find? Write them in German words. Which number was hardest to say?
success_check: I can say my age in German.
I can say my phone number in pairs of digits.
I can say five numbers between 21 and 99 in German.
mission.safety_note: Use a made-up phone number or only practise alone. Do not share your real phone number, address or other personal data online.
